item.title: Easement Dispute Stalls Office Conversion Above Chicago JW Marriott
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
A foreclosed hotel owner sues to stop an office-to-residential conversion above the JW Marriott Chicago, citing a violated easement agreement.

The post Easement Dispute Stalls Office Conversion Above Chicago JW Marriott appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
A lender that foreclosed on the JW Marriott Chicago in 2022 has sued to halt an office-to-residential conversion of five floors at 208 South LaSalle Street, claiming the project violates a 2014 reciprocal easement agreement. The developer began demolition work in late October to prepare the conversion, which is part of Mayor Brandon Johnson’s LaSalle Street Reimagined Initiative. The hotel occupies the 12 floors below the office space being converted into apartments in the landmark building.

The lawsuit centers on a reciprocal easement agreement that requires either party to obtain consent before undertaking work that could materially affect the other. The hotel’s owner argues the developer proceeded without obtaining that approval. A hearing in the case is scheduled for January 4, 2027, though that date appears to be far in the future.

The LaSalle Street Reimagined Initiative launched after the pandemic emptied Loop office buildings, with city officials aiming to transform what they called an “office monoculture” into a mixed-use neighborhood. The Bellweather Residences, the first completed conversion under the program, opened in early September. The 208 South LaSalle dispute illustrates how easement agreements and shared infrastructure can complicate adaptive reuse projects even when municipal policy supports them.

JW Marriott Sues LaSalle Street Reimagined Developer Over Office-To-Residential Conversion

item.title: States Are Funding Housing With Debt Instead of Rule Changes
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
Rising borrowing costs threaten housing bond economics

The post States Are Funding Housing With Debt Instead of Rule Changes appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
1 hr 23 min agoNov. 9, 2026 2:22 pm

Six state housing measures appeared on ballots last week, the most in a single election year since at least 2006, and the results split cleanly along one line. Voters approved every measure that asked them to borrow money for housing and rejected both measures that asked them to loosen the rules governing where housing can be built.

California carried the bulk of the borrowing. Proposition 1 authorized $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds with about 59 percent support, sending $7.2 billion to affordable multifamily housing, $1.1 billion to homeownership assistance, and smaller allocations to farmworker, student, tribal, and infrastructure programs, plus $1.25 billion for veteran home loans. Proposition 37 passed with 61 percent, authorizing up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for second mortgages covering as much as 17 percent of a new home’s price. Rhode Island approved a $120 million housing bond with more than 61 percent, its second in two cycles after a $120 million measure cleared with 65 percent in 2024. Hawaii voters amended the state constitution with about 62 percent to let counties issue Resilient Infrastructure for Shelter and Equity bonds, a tax increment mechanism repaid from property tax growth inside designated districts rather than from general funds. Raleigh passed a $101.5 million housing bond with nearly 65 percent.

Both regulatory measures failed. California’s Proposition 45, which would have streamlined permitting and environmental review under a law now half a century old, went down with nearly 56 percent opposed. Massachusetts Question 7 would have allowed a single-family home on any residentially zoned lot outside Boston measuring at least 5,000 square feet with road frontage and utility connections, and it had backing from Governor Maura Healey and Boston Mayor Michelle Wu. Jesse Kanson-Benanav, executive director of Abundant Housing Massachusetts, had argued the current standards push builders toward larger and costlier houses, describing the state’s average minimum lot as closer in size to an NFL field than an NBA court. Opponents ran on local control and the absence of affordability guardrails, and they won.

Borrowing was the cheaper option the last time most of these states went to voters. State and local governments issued a record $611.8 billion in municipal bonds over the 52 weeks ending October 16, according to Bloomberg data compiled by Matt Fabian, president of Municipal Market Analytics. SIFMA put issuance through October at $521 billion against $4.5 trillion outstanding. September brought the worst municipal selloff since the financial crisis, pushing the underlying yield on the broad muni index to its highest level since 2008, and the supply has been widening spreads against Treasuries at the long end of the curve.

California’s Legislative Analyst’s Office estimated repayment on the $10 billion general housing portion of Proposition 1 at $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years, roughly a quarter of one percent of the General Fund, with total cost running about 15 percent above what paying up front would have required. The veterans portion repays itself through participant mortgage payments. That estimate predates the recent move in yields, and every measure that passed last week carries a schedule of its own arriving in budgets already absorbing the end of pandemic-era federal aid.

Melina Lodge, executive director of the Housing Network of Rhode Island, has defended the approach on the grounds that development costs have outrun what private capital will fund at lower price points, leaving bonds as the only reliable source for units the market will not build on its own. Rhode Island’s business-backed policy council pushed back during the campaign, questioning whether the state’s recent housing spending had produced enough homes to justify what it cost.

Money raised through a bond spreads across every taxpayer over decades and buys something visible. A lot size standard asks the person voting to accept a change on their own street for the benefit of someone who does not live there yet. The second proposition is harder to sell, which both results confirm. What makes Massachusetts worth watching is how close it came anyway, in a state with some of the highest housing costs in the country, on a ballot where it finished tighter than eight other questions.

The post States Are Funding Housing With Debt Instead of Rule Changes appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Out-of-State Capital Returns to San Francisco’s Office Market
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Florida investment firm 1754 Properties paid $28 million for San Francisco office building, plans more deals as AI boom attracts out-of-state capital.

The post Out-of-State Capital Returns to San Francisco’s Office Market appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Florida-based 1754 Properties closed on a six-story office building at 40 Jessie Street in late October for nearly $28 million, marking the firm’s first San Francisco acquisition and first office purchase in a portfolio otherwise concentrated in Florida and Mexico hotels. The company partnered with Vander Capital Partners on the deal, which values the property roughly $10 million above the $17.6 million Long Market Property Partners paid Golden Gate University in 2023. Google occupies the entire building under a lease that runs through 2030, following its 2021 acquisition of previous tenant Fitbit. About 60% of the space is configured as lab area.

1754 Properties CEO Joe Smith said the firm plans to build a larger Bay Area office portfolio and is seeking local partners for additional deals. He cited the city’s AI-driven leasing momentum and office vacancy falling below 30% as evidence the market has turned. Smith called current conditions “probably the best it’s been in 12 years” and expects single-digit vacancy rates within four to five years. The firm is passing on hotel investments in San Francisco despite its specialty in that sector, citing high union concentration and labor costs.

San Francisco has drawn a wave of out-of-state buyers over the past year as AI growth has shifted investor sentiment. A Texas investor began acquiring Union Square properties in 2023, while East Coast investors launched Project Uris in the same neighborhood. Foreign capital entered the market this year with purchases of the Transamerica Pyramid and Ghirardelli Square, and a New York investor is set to buy a downtown retail property. Smith described the shift as a reversal of the prior five years, when capital flowed from California to Florida rather than the opposite direction.

item.title: Leadership Turnover Tests Blackstone’s Real Estate Division After Years of Decline
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Blackstone's real estate division installs new co-heads after leadership exodus, with profits halved since 2022 and a flagship fundraise delayed.

The post Leadership Turnover Tests Blackstone’s Real Estate Division After Years of Decline appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Blackstone named David Levine and Giovanni Cutaia as co-heads of its real estate division in September, following Nadeem Meghji’s departure after less than ten months as sole leader. Meghji, who succeeded Kathleen McCarthy in January, plans to leave by year-end to spend time with family before pursuing new ventures. Jon Gray, Blackstone’s president who built the real estate group, attempted to persuade Meghji to stay but failed. The leadership shuffle comes as the division struggles with declining profits and a delayed $30 billion fundraise.

Blackstone’s real estate group posted distributable earnings down 10% year-over-year in the most recent quarter, with opportunistic strategies losing 3.2% in three months. Assets under management have dropped $30 billion from peak levels to roughly $309 billion as of September 30. The division’s profit now runs at half its 2022 peak, and private equity has overtaken real estate as Blackstone’s most profitable business. The flagship BREP IX fund, which began investing in 2019, has generated annualized net returns of just 3%.

Levine and Cutaia inherit nearly $47 billion in dry powder awaiting deployment across a dozen portfolios, with nearly one-third sitting in the flagship global real estate fund. That fund must deploy at least 70% of its $30 billion before Blackstone can raise new capital from investors. Recent bright spots include data center sales in Northern Virginia and AI-driven demand for warehouses and office space, with Anthropic leasing a 25-story San Francisco tower. Other major firms face similar challenges, with KKR and Carlyle posting comparable low-single-digit returns on pandemic-era opportunistic funds.

High interest rates continue to freeze commercial real estate transactions, with sellers unwilling to accept lower valuations and buyers waiting for better entry points. Blackstone is running a secondary process for its Blackstone Property Partners fund to return cash to investors and has cut management fees for some who remain. The new co-heads plan to focus on warehouses, hotels, grocery-anchored retail, and data center funding, but acknowledge capital markets headwinds from rate volatility. Gray maintains confidence in AI infrastructure investments tied to long-term contracts with hyperscalers, though new political headwinds may emerge from Democrats’ midterm gains and Senator Elizabeth Warren’s expected Senate Banking Committee chairmanship.

Bloomberg
Blackstone Real Estate Seeks Rebound From Shock Exits and Losses

item.title: What Owners Can Learn From How Lenders Handle Property Taxes
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Studio
item.description:
Commercial real estate owners can reduce property tax delinquency risks with automated monitoring, API connectivity, and smarter payment systems.

The post What Owners Can Learn From How Lenders Handle Property Taxes appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Residential mortgage servicing largely solved the property tax problem decades ago by escrowing the payment. The servicer collects monthly, holds the funds, tracks the obligation, and pays the authority. Nobody has to remember anything.

Commercial real estate works differently. A substantial share of commercial loans are structured without escrow, leaving the borrower to pay taxes directly. For sophisticated sponsors with good systems, that arrangement makes sense and preserves cash flow flexibility. What it also does is remove the mechanism that would otherwise catch a missed payment, which means the first indication something went wrong is often a delinquency notice or a lien filing.

The exposure compounds when liquidity gets tight. Bills arrive semiannually or annually, enforcement is not immediate, and a borrower in triage mode treats a deferred tax payment as an interest-free float while debt service and operating costs take priority. That dynamic turns routine tax cycles into sudden balance-sheet exposure for the lenders and servicers holding the paper.

What makes a tax delinquency different from other missed obligations is where it sits in the capital stack. Unpaid property taxes carry statutory first-lien priority ahead of the mortgage, and jurisdictions routinely apply penalty and interest rates of 12 to 18 percent or higher on delinquent balances. Commercial tax delinquency runs between 1 and 3 percent in major metropolitan markets, which adds up to more than $3 billion in unpaid taxes annually.

For an owner, the range of outcomes is wide and the bad end of it is genuinely bad. “For many owners the best case scenario is tens of thousands of dollars of fines,” said Aaron Eichenlaub, Senior Vice President of Commercial Payment Solutions at Cotality. “Worst case is a tax lien sale.”

Getting there usually takes more than one failure, and Eichenlaub describes the exposure as stacked rather than singular. “There are a few layers of risk,” he said. The first sits outside the organization entirely. “One is just missing an update. Things like jurisdiction rules, valuations, and deadlines can change, especially when you own properties across multiple taxing authorities.” A reassessment notice or a changed filing deadline arrives by mail, with no confirmation that anyone read it.

The second layer is internal. “The other risk is having someone on the team misinput the data or drop the ball on making the changes altogether,” Eichenlaub said. A notice that arrives correctly and gets entered wrong produces the same outcome as one nobody opened.

Neither layer gets caught by the monitoring most portfolios actually run. Annual sample audits, post-delinquency notifications, and manual checks across fragmented assessor portals are reactive by design. By the time a missed payment shows up in that process, penalties have been accruing and the problem is being managed rather than prevented.

Lenders have had to solve this because escrow administration made it their operational responsibility first. Servicing loans against properties scattered across dozens of states meant building the capability to track obligations in every jurisdiction those properties sat in, and that work produced a discipline that most owners never needed to develop.

“The lenders have operationalized understanding risk better,” Eichenlaub said. “They are much better at thinking about it not as a data point and more as a process since they know how taxes can change.” A tax figure captured at acquisition holds until something changes, which in practice is not long. Treating it as a standing obligation that requires monitoring produces different systems than treating it as a number in an underwriting model.

The most useful recent development has been direct connectivity to the authorities themselves. By partnering with tech companies that have created APIs with participating taxing authorities, real estate companies can remove the lag between when something changes and when anyone knows about it. “API connectivity from the taxing authorities helps provide the timely updates needed to stay ahead of changes,” Eichenlaub said. “We have seen a huge uptick in API adoption from property tax authorities in cities and counties across the country.” Adoption has been uneven across the roughly 22,000 taxing authorities operating in the United States. Cotality maintains connections across that full set and acts as a fiduciary on the payments it processes, which runs to roughly $30 billion annually.

Centralizing that monitoring also removes a category of work that occupies capable people without producing much. Confirming a payment cleared, chasing a receipt, reconciling a refund, and verifying that an assessment change made it into the system are all necessary and none require the judgment of an experienced accountant. “Validating payments, confirmations, and refunds can take a lot of time away from other important jobs,” Eichenlaub said. “By partnering with a firm that can do that for them they can really find some extra time for accountants and managers to work on other, higher value tasks.”

Non-escrow arrangements make sense for plenty of borrowers and will continue to. What they remove is the tracking mechanism that escrow provided by default, and the portfolios carrying that exposure are often monitoring it with annual audits and manual checks across jurisdictions that change their rules without warning. Lenders built better systems because the first-lien priority of a tax delinquency made it their problem. Owners facing the same priority can now use the same tools and the same strategy as lenders to help them keep their property tax risks to a minimum.

item.title: Industrial’s Demand Caught Up. Now Comes the Hard Part.
item.dc:creator: Travis Barrington
item.description:
U.S. industrial real estate is rebounding in 2026, but uneven demand, rising rates and new supply pose risks heading into 2027.

The post Industrial’s Demand Caught Up. Now Comes the Hard Part. appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
For most of the past three years, industrial real estate had a simple math problem. Developers built too much, too fast, and tenants couldn’t absorb it all. The only question was how high vacancy would climb.

That question now has an answer. According to Savills’ State of the U.S. Industrial Market report for Q3 2026, net absorption outpaced new deliveries by 7.0% through the first three quarters of the year. National vacancy has slipped to 8.0%, down 20 basis points from its 8.2% peak. And leasing totaled 543.7 million square feet across Q2 and Q3, the strongest two-quarter stretch Savills has on record.

Q3 alone saw 80 million square feet of net absorption, more than double the 38.9 msf posted a year earlier. Sublease availability, usually an early warning sign, is down 13.6% year over year after peaking at a record 196.5 msf. By most measures, the market has turned a corner.

But look past the national averages and the picture gets more complicated. The recovery is uneven by building size, by quality and by geography. And rising interest rates threaten to cool it before it fully takes hold.

A new kind of tenant

The tenant mix says a lot about where this cycle is headed. Among the largest deals Savills tracked over the past four quarters, logistics firms and 3PLs accounted for 37% of leasing. Manufacturers were close behind at 27%. E-commerce, the engine of the pandemic boom, took just 10%.

Online retail hasn’t stalled. E-commerce penetration hit a new record in Q2, up 80 bps from a year earlier. But the marginal tenant looks different now. Savills counted 78,117 jobs announced in large U.S. manufacturing projects over the trailing 12 months, up 46.6% year over year, with announced capital investment more than doubling to $69.5 billion. Just as important, the share of announced jobs tied to stalled or canceled projects has dropped to 11.3%, after spiking above 70% around the start of 2025.

Defense is adding fuel. Aerospace and defense venture funding is on pace for $51.1 billion this year, 186% above its five-year average. Companies like Anduril, Hadrian and Saronic are raising billions to build physical things, and physical things need factories and warehouses.

Then there is the data center supply chain. Savills highlights a string of big-box leases signed by companies that cool, power and equip data centers. Stellar Energy Americas, a Trane subsidiary making modular cooling gear, took 1.15 msf in Dallas-Fort Worth. Google signed two Atlanta leases totaling roughly 1.5 msf.

Our read: Houston is the quiet winner of this trend. Five of the 12 data center-related leases in Savills’ list landed there, adding up to about 3 million square feet. That’s the city’s energy-equipment expertise being repurposed for the AI power trade. The catch is that this demand rides on a development boom facing its own headwinds. Savills notes that 40% of data center projects slated for 2026 completion risk delays of three months or more, and 16 states have considered bans or moratoriums. Landlords leasing to its suppliers take on secondhand exposure to those risks.

A two-speed market

National averages hide a market that is splitting along three lines.

Size. Vacancy in buildings of 750,000 square feet and up fell 130 bps over the past year to 6.5%, making big-box the tightest segment in the country. Vacancy in 50,000 to 200,000 sf buildings rose 60 bps to 8.6%. That flips the conventional wisdom of the last cycle, when small-bay was considered the scarce, safe corner of the market. The tenants driving this recovery, from consolidating 3PLs to new manufacturing plants, want scale. Small-bay depends more on small businesses, which tend to feel higher borrowing costs first.

Quality. Class A vacancy, which swelled during the delivery wave, has been falling all year. Class B and C space, meanwhile, has logged 13 consecutive quarters of net occupancy losses. Office owners will recognize this flight to quality, and its warning: older buildings may not get pulled along.

Geography. Nine markets are now leasing at 90% or more of their prior peak, up from just one a year ago. Dallas-Fort Worth leads at 130% of its 10-year peak. By our math, DFW absorbed 18% of the nation’s net absorption this year (35.7 msf) while holding only about 5% of its inventory. Columbus cut vacancy by 210 bps, the most of any major market.

The West Coast is the outlier. Its rents are down 20.9% from their 2023 peak, and Seattle/Puget Sound posted the largest vacancy increase among major markets, up 260 bps to 12.7%. Overbuilding is part of the story, but so is trade. West Coast ports handled 55% of top-nine port volume in 2016; today it’s roughly an even split with the East and Gulf Coasts. The Northwest Seaport Alliance’s volume is down 31.9% since 2019. When the cargo moves, the warehouse demand follows.

Austin offers a cautionary note in the other direction. Leasing there is running at 117% of its prior peak, yet vacancy sits at 16.1%, the highest among the major markets Savills charts. With 11.8 msf under construction, roughly 9% of existing inventory by our calculation, even record demand can’t outrun that much supply.

Rents are rising, just not in real terms

The national asking rent reached $9.79 per square foot in Q3, up 2.5% from a year ago. But inflation hit 3.6% in September, which means industrial rents fell roughly 1% in real terms over the past year.

The growth that does exist is concentrated in lower-cost markets. Washington, DC led with 13.2% annual rent growth, followed by Columbus at 12.0% and Dallas-Fort Worth at 11.0%. The pricey coastal markets moved the other way, with the Inland Empire down 11.6%, Orange County down 9.7% and Los Angeles down 7.7%.

Concessions tell a similar story. On large warehouse leases, free rent has averaged 4.8 months in 2026, up 81.6% since 2022, according to CompStak data in the Savills report. That figure has finally flattened, but effective rents still lag well behind face rents.

The less-discussed number is escalations. Average annual rent bumps have eased from a peak near 3.8% in 2023 to 3.5% today. With inflation now running at 3.6%, even a brand-new lease is barely keeping pace. Owners holding leases signed in 2018 through 2020, when escalations averaged about 2.7%, are watching their real income erode every year those leases stay in place.

Capital is back, with a thin cushion

Investors have noticed the turn. Warehouse sales reached $93.3 billion through Q3, the strongest first nine months on record, edging out 2021’s $92.9 billion. Refinancings hit a record $86.9 billion over the four quarters ending in Q2. Industrial prices remain 24.9% above where they were five years ago, and the sector’s CMBS delinquency rate sits at just 1.1%, compared with 12.2% for office.

The number that should give buyers pause is the spread. Savills reports that the gap between top-quartile warehouse cap rates and the 10-year Treasury is 120 bps below its 10-year average. Investors are paying up for the recovery story while leaving little room for error.

Put that next to the rent data and the bet becomes clear. Buyers are underwriting future rent growth to justify thin spreads at a moment when real rents are falling. If the 10-year keeps climbing with inflation, something has to give: cap rates expand, or rent growth has to accelerate quickly. Record refinancing volume suggests many owners see the risk and are locking in debt while they can.

The next supply test

The biggest risk to this recovery may be the recovery itself. Construction starts reached 79.4 msf in Q3, pushing the national pipeline to 321.6 msf, up 10.2% from a year earlier. Savills found speculative construction rising in three out of four markets, led by Columbus (up 7.7 msf) and Houston (up 6.6 msf).

At this year’s absorption pace, that pipeline equals about 15 months of demand by our math. That is manageable nationally, but the build-up is concentrated in the markets with the best leasing stories. Columbus, with some of the country’s fastest rent growth, now has 13.7 msf underway, about 4.4% of its inventory and more than twice the national ratio.

Higher rates may impose the discipline developers won’t. SOFR has turned back up, and Savills suggests build-to-suit projects, now 22.4% of the pipeline, may become more common as speculative development gets harder to finance.

The industrial market solved its oversupply problem by outrunning it. The question heading into 2027 is whether it can avoid recreating that problem. Demand is real and broadening, from 3PLs and factories to defense contractors and data center suppliers. But money is getting more expensive, real rents are slipping and the spread cushion is thin. The owners best positioned for what comes next hold large, modern buildings in markets where leasing is surging and pipelines stayed in check. Everyone else is still waiting for the recovery to reach them.

The post Industrial’s Demand Caught Up. Now Comes the Hard Part. appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Congressional Democrats Target Equipment Expensing Rules for Data Centers
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Democratic lawmakers propose ending bonus depreciation for data center equipment, raising $30 billion as political opposition to the sector intensifies nationwide.

The post Congressional Democrats Target Equipment Expensing Rules for Data Centers appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Democratic lawmakers have introduced multiple bills to eliminate bonus depreciation for data center equipment, a tax provision that allows developers to immediately expense server racks, GPUs, and other capital costs rather than deduct them over the equipment’s lifetime. Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia introduced the Data Center Tax Accountability and Disclosure Act in July, which would raise nearly $30 billion over 10 years by barring full expensing for data center owners. Senate Finance Ranking Member Ron Wyden of Oregon proposed going further, blocking data centers from Opportunity Zone incentives and REIT benefits in addition to bonus depreciation. Rep. Chris Pappas of New Hampshire, who won election to the Senate this week, has also introduced legislation targeting the same tax treatment.

Democrats gained control of Congress in the recent midterm elections, though any legislation must still pass President Trump. Tax policy experts at the Tax Foundation and BDO note that while full expensing under Section 168(k) has enjoyed bipartisan support for manufacturers and other industries, the proposals targeting data centers reflect a broader political backlash against the sector. Andrew Lautz of the Tax Foundation said the energy behind these bills is directed specifically at data centers, not at equipment expensing more broadly. The proposals may set the agenda for future tax legislation if Democrats regain the presidency.

Opposition to data centers has grown sharply over the past year, with 47 local ballot measures limiting AI data center development passing in the midterm elections. Permit approval rates for data centers fell to 34% in the third quarter from 54% in 2025, according to Spark. Polling from Heatmap shows 75% of Americans now oppose data centers near their homes, up from 42% in August 2025. Developers face more restrictive zoning, permitting requirements, and demands for community benefits even as over $1 trillion in capital flows into data center construction nationwide.

A Data-Center-Friendly Tax Credit May Become a Target in 2027

item.title: A Blue Wave Meets a Veto Pen: What the Midterms Mean for CRE
item.dc:creator: Travis Barrington
item.description:
Democrats swept Congress, but Trump’s veto means the energy and tax changes affecting commercial real estate are likely to stand through 2028.

The post A Blue Wave Meets a Veto Pen: What the Midterms Mean for CRE appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Democrats will take control of both chambers of Congress in January after an election night that went worse for Republicans than almost anyone in either party predicted. As of Wednesday morning they had secured at least 228 House seats and 54 Senate seats, with dozens of House races still being counted and network projections running considerably higher. The Senate map was the biggest surprise, with Democrats flipping seats in Kansas, Iowa, Texas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina, several of which were not considered competitive a year ago. About two-thirds of voters told an election-day survey that tariffs had hurt the economy, and gas prices tied to the war with Iran weighed on Republican candidates almost everywhere.

Markets mostly shrugged. Stock futures dipped overnight before recovering, the 10-year Treasury yield fell a few basis points to between 4.90% and 4.94%, and oil and the dollar both slipped modestly, according to Cushman & Wakefield. Investors seem to understand that winning Congress and governing from it are very different things while Donald Trump still holds the veto.

Trump made that point himself on election night, posting an image of a red cap with “VETO” stitched across the front. On Wednesday he told reporters that Democrats would “send over things that are insane and I’ll veto them,” though he also said he expected to work with the new majority on some issues. Overriding a veto requires two-thirds of both chambers, which means 290 votes in the House and 67 in the Senate, and Democrats are nowhere near either number. Most legislation also has to clear a Senate filibuster that requires 60 votes. Budget reconciliation gets around the filibuster with a simple majority, but a reconciliation bill still ends up on the president’s desk.

Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become Speaker, has promised to restore Medicaid funding and Affordable Care Act subsidies, roll back tariffs and end the war with Iran. Each of those goals depends on Trump signing something he opposes or on enough Republicans breaking with him to override his veto. Some defections are plausible, since Trump is in his final two years and Republicans who just watched colleagues lose in Kansas and Texas have reason to keep some distance from the White House, particularly on tariffs. Getting to two-thirds is another matter, and party discipline usually erodes one narrow vote at a time.

For commercial real estate, the federal policies with the most direct effect on buildings are already written into law. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed in July 2025, cut short much of the Inflation Reduction Act’s clean energy package. Owners felt it most through Section 179D, the energy-efficient commercial buildings deduction, which does not apply to projects that began construction after June 30, 2026. The 45L credit for efficient new homes and the 30C credit for EV charging equipment ran into similar deadlines. Bringing any of them back would take a new tax bill with Trump’s signature on it, which is unlikely before he leaves office. The same law made 100% bonus depreciation permanent, a provision the industry lobbied hard for, and Democrats can’t repeal it over his objection any more than they can restore 179D. Owners can reasonably assume the tax code they are working with today is the one they will have in 2028.

Tariffs rest on executive power rather than legislation. After the Supreme Court struck down the emergency tariffs in February, the administration reissued them under other trade authorities that Congress had delegated years ago. A Democratic Congress can hold hearings and apply pressure, but it cannot change that policy on its own, so the cost of steel, aluminum and other building materials will keep following decisions made at the White House.

Where Democrats do gain real power is in their ability to slow things down. Control of both chambers gives them appropriations, committee chairmanships and subpoena authority, and Cushman & Wakefield expects divided government to raise the odds of a debt-limit fight, government shutdowns and more unilateral trade action from the executive branch. The White House has reportedly spent months preparing to advance its agenda without going through Congress at all. Policy made by executive order can change quickly and be reversed just as quickly, and that kind of uncertainty is harder for lenders and investors to price than a statute that will sit on the books for years.

The larger variable for property values is the war. Vice President JD Vance blamed Tuesday’s losses on the Iran conflict, and Trump pointed to gas prices. Cushman & Wakefield considers the war the primary swing factor for inflation and interest rates, and in a market priced off the 10-year Treasury, that matters more than which party runs the House.

Past midterms offer little reason to expect a shift in property markets. Since 1978, private real estate returns in the year following a midterm have looked about the same as returns in any other year, according to Cushman & Wakefield, and REITs, which reprice faster, show the same pattern. The firm did not change its economic outlook after Tuesday, because a divided Congress was already part of its baseline. It expects growth slightly above 2%, inflation that stays elevated before gradually easing, and a 10-year yield between 4.5% and 5.0% through 2027.

That outlook is reasonably good for occupiers. Continued growth should support demand for space across most property types, and with little new construction in the pipeline, rents should rise, especially in the highest-quality buildings. For investors, Cushman & Wakefield expects returns to come from rising income rather than falling cap rates, so interest rates, economic growth and the performance of individual properties will matter far more over the next two years than anything that happens on Capitol Hill.

item.title: Cross-Border Property Losses Trigger Criminal Probe at German Pension Fund
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Munich prosecutors raided an asset manager over US property investments that may cost Germany's largest public pension fund €853 million.

The post Cross-Border Property Losses Trigger Criminal Probe at German Pension Fund appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Munich prosecutors raided Deutsche Finance on Tuesday as part of an investigation into US real estate investments that produced substantial losses for BVK, Germany’s largest public-sector pension fund. BVK oversees €122 billion in retirement assets for 2.8 million Bavarians and has flagged potential write-offs of as much as €853 million on US properties linked to Deutsche Finance and New York developer Michael Shvo’s firm SHVO. Deutsche Finance confirmed the search and said it is cooperating as a third party, while prosecutors declined to specify the focus of their probe. Süddeutsche Zeitung reported the investigation centers on allegations of bribery through trips and amenities.

BVK invested roughly €1.6 billion in a portfolio of US trophy assets including the Transamerica Pyramid in San Francisco, 685 Fifth Avenue and 711 Fifth Avenue in New York, 9200 Wilshire Boulevard in Los Angeles, and 333 South Wabash in Chicago. By the end of last year, the pension group had already written off €392 million of those investments. SHVO said earlier this year that the properties are outperforming the market with record rents and blue-chip tenants, while Deutsche Finance said in January that its US subsidiary had no discretionary authority over investment selection or execution.

Two senior BVK managers departed after an internal investigation found compliance violations, including lavish business trips. German prosecutors have not accused Shvo or his firm of wrongdoing, and neither Deutsche Finance nor the prosecutors mentioned SHVO in their Tuesday communications. Germany’s vocational pension fund industry, which manages roughly €300 billion in retirement savings, operates under fragmented supervision and is often overseen by people with limited investing experience.

Several German vocational pension funds have surfaced as backers of US real estate developments and other investments that faltered when interest rates rose. BVK’s losses have intensified scrutiny of governance practices across the €300 billion sector, which forms a critical piece of Germany’s retirement infrastructure. The Munich prosecutors’ office said it will release additional details on the investigation in the coming days.

German Raid Adds to Scrutiny of Pension Fund’s US Property Deals

item.title: Four Brokerages Form Shared Listing System to Counter Compass Strategy
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
AGNT, HomeServices, Keller Williams and REMAX back Open Real Estate, a shared listing platform challenging Compass's private-listing strategy amid federal lawsuits.

The post Four Brokerages Form Shared Listing System to Counter Compass Strategy appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
AGNT, HomeServices of America, Keller Williams and Real REMAX Group announced Oct. 26 they are backing Open Real Estate, a shared listing platform designed to distribute property data across multiple listing services and authorized websites. Participating brokerages would be required to submit new listings within one business day of signing a seller agreement. Brown Harris Stevens, Lamacchia Realty, Samson Properties and Windermere are among the initial participants, with the four founding companies covering the cost of building the technology at no initial charge to members.

Six regional multiple listing services representing more than 120,000 real estate professionals filed a federal lawsuit against Compass last month seeking to enforce rules requiring brokers to share property listings. OneKey MLS in New York has since joined a separate lawsuit brought by California Regional Multiple Listing Service. Compass has expanded its private-listing network, arguing that homeowners should control when and how their properties are advertised; the company’s research shows sellers who first marketed properties as Private Exclusives or Coming Soons achieved sale prices 4.6% higher than comparable homes listed directly on the MLS and went under contract 34% faster.

Open Real Estate includes a “participant view” feature allowing certain properties to be shared exclusively among agents at participating brokerages without public marketing, similar to a system used by the Real Estate Board of New York. Brown Harris Stevens CEO Bess Freedman said the feature would accommodate a small percentage of sellers requesting privacy for security or personal reasons, while the broader platform aims to prevent data hoarding. Compass CEO Robert Reffkin said the new national listing service would return greater control to homeowners and their agents, and Open Real Estate’s founders said Compass would be welcome to join the platform.

The initiative comes after Compass completed a $1.6 billion merger with Anywhere Real Estate, bringing major brokerage brands under the same corporate umbrella. Open Real Estate would operate alongside existing multiple listing services rather than replace them. A Compass spokesperson said the company is challenging industry rules so homeowners can market their homes publicly even if they choose channels other than the MLS or Zillow, arguing that the law does not require homeowners to give those private companies their data.
